clue.text: Author of satirical works placed in covers, perhaps

definitions.meaning: Henry ... wrote satires such as Shamela and Joseph Andrews
in cricket, a player stationed at cover point is out in the field, and covers is one such position

explanation.walkthrough: Cover (or covers) is a cricket fielding position on the off side; 'perhaps' marks it as one example among many.
explanation.definitionFit: The novelist Henry Fielding mocked Richardson in parody, and a cricketer posted at cover is out in the field.

clue.text: Poet, one anguished about onset of war

indicators.note: about means the rearranged letters go round the next piece
something anguished is twisted in torment, so these letters are wrung into a new order
onset of means only the opening letter of the word war is used

explanation.surface: A poet, tormented by the coming of war, writes about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'anguished' turns ONE into OEN, and 'about' puts it round W, the first letter of war (from 'onset of').
explanation.definitionFit: Wilfred Owen is the celebrated First World War poet.

clue.text: Creator of bloodthirsty character, one adding fuel to the fire

definitions.meaning: Bram ... wrote Dracula, whose vampire drinks blood

definitions.text: one adding fuel to the fire
definitions.meaning: a person who feeds coal into a furnace, as on a steam engine

explanation.definitionFit: Bram Stoker created the vampire Count Dracula, and a fireman who shovels coal into a boiler has the same title.

clue.text: US author that could make King Lear fun

indicators.note: could make says these letters can be rearranged to form the answer

parts.note: K is the chess abbreviation for king
taken as written

explanation.surface: Suggests an American novelist might turn Shakespeare's tragedy into comedy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'could make' rearranges K (King), LEAR and FUN: eight letters, so the whole of King is not used.
explanation.definitionFit: William Faulkner was an American novelist from Mississippi, a Nobel laureate.

clue.text: Singer and philosopher securing new book

indicators.note: securing means the pair of words holds the next piece fast between them

parts.note: an alto is a singer with a low female or high male voice
John Locke was an English philosopher

explanation.surface: A vocalist and a thinker together guard a freshly published volume.
explanation.walkthrough: 'securing' marks the container. The book is a novel by Charles Kingsley, a Victorian clergyman-author.
explanation.definitionFit: Alton Locke is an 1850 novel by Charles Kingsley, so it names a particular book.

clue.text: Victorian author's only novel, about abstainer

indicators.note: about means the rearranged letters go round the next piece
novel means new or unusual, so the letters of only appear in a fresh order

parts.note: TT, teetotal, describes someone who abstains from alcohol

explanation.surface: Says a Victorian writer produced just one book, about a teetotaller.
explanation.walkthrough: 'novel' turns ONLY into LYON, and 'about' places it round TT. The 's stands for 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Edward Bulwer-Lytton was a prolific Victorian novelist, author of The Last Days of Pompeii.

clue.text: Poetic Indian greeting what's revised in articles

parts.note: hi is an informal greeting

indicators.note: in means the reworked letters go inside the two articles

parts.note: A and A are two indefinite articles

indicators.note: revised means changed, so the letters of what are reworded

parts.note: the word what, its 's no letter here

explanation.surface: A verse Indian is welcomed in some edited pieces of writing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revised' signals the anagram and 'in' the container; A and A are the indefinite article taken twice.
explanation.definitionFit: Hiawatha is the Native American hero of Longfellow's narrative poem.

clue.text: Later poet adapted pieces from Landor

indicators.note: adapted pieces from says the bits of the name Landor are reworked into another name

explanation.surface: A subsequent poet reworked passages taken from Walter Savage Landor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'adapted pieces from' rearranges LANDOR. Matthew Arnold came after the poet Landor, hence 'Later'.
explanation.definitionFit: Matthew Arnold was a Victorian poet, younger than Walter Savage Landor.

clue.text: Elizabethan actor of the old school has name put on marble

definitions.text: Elizabethan actor of the old school

indicators.note: put on means the second piece is attached at the end of the first

parts.note: an alley is a large playing marble

explanation.surface: An actor from Shakespeare's era gets his name engraved in marble.
explanation.walkthrough: Edward Alleyn founded Dulwich College in London, so he is literally of the old school.
explanation.definitionFit: Edward Alleyn was a leading Elizabethan actor and the founder of Dulwich College, a school.

clue.text: Female novelist making daringly naughty contribution

indicators.note: a contribution is a part given by the whole phrase, so letters are taken from inside daringly naughty

explanation.surface: A woman writer produces some bold, racy work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'contribution' takes the letters running across daringly naughty. Elinor Glyn wrote risqué romances.
explanation.definitionFit: Elinor Glyn was an Edwardian romantic novelist noted for daring fiction.

clue.text: The work especially about love that Scott wrote

indicators.note: about means the rearranged letters go round the next piece
especially read as specially made, so these letters are put into a new order

parts.note: love is nil, a zero score in tennis

explanation.surface: Describes a novel by Walter Scott, chiefly concerned with romance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'especially', read as specially made, signals the anagram of KEWORTH-style letters; 'about' wraps them round the score for love in tennis. Kenilworth is a castle in Warwickshire.
explanation.definitionFit: Kenilworth is an 1821 historical novel by Sir Walter Scott.

clue.text: Dramatist gets nothing from clue

indicators.note: from means the next piece is taken away out of the following word

parts.note: a pointer is a hint or clue
O, a zero, represents nothing

explanation.surface: A playwright receives an empty hint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from' takes O out of POINTER.
explanation.definitionFit: Harold Pinter was a Nobel-winning British playwright.

clue.text: Duke, say, with young attendants — they're bound to be at the front

definitions.text: they're bound to be at the front

parts.note: Duke is an example of a title of nobility
pages are boys who serve as attendants

explanation.surface: A nobleman with his retinue of boys, who must lead the way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bound' is a pun: title pages are bound into the front of books, not obliged to be there.
explanation.definitionFit: The leaf naming a book sits in the binding at its very start.

clue.text: Old poet's point of view mostly embraced by country

indicators.note: embraced by means the shortened word sits inside the next piece

parts.note: a land is a country

indicators.note: mostly means the last letter of the word is dropped

parts.note: an angle is a viewpoint or slant

explanation.surface: An early poet's outlook was largely shaped by his nation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mostly' cuts ANGLE to ANGL, and 'embraced by' sets it inside LAND. The 's stands for 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: William Langland wrote Piers Plowman in the fourteenth century.

clue.text: Game backed by great man of American literature

indicators.note: backed means the word is read in the reverse direction

parts.note: stags are deer, hunted as game

explanation.surface: Says a sport was supported by a major American writer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backed' signals the reversal. The hero of Fitzgerald's novel is the Great Gatsby, hence 'great man'.
explanation.definitionFit: Fitzgerald's hero is literally titled the Great Gatsby, a famous man of US fiction.

clue.text: Book published in good shape for one of the Brontës

parts.note: a newspaper ran a story when it published it
well means healthy, in good shape

explanation.surface: A book appears and is in fine condition, linked to a literary family.
explanation.definitionFit: Branwell Brontë was the brother of Charlotte, Emily and Anne.

clue.text: Authentic German associated with Berlin rep, primarily

definitions.text: Authentic German associated with Berlin rep, primarily

indicators.note: primarily means only the first letters of Berlin and rep are used

parts.note: echt is German for genuine or authentic

explanation.surface: A true German figure connected with a Berlin repertory theatre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'primarily' gives B and R; then ECHT. Bertolt Brecht founded the Berliner Ensemble, a repertory company.
explanation.definitionFit: Bertolt Brecht was a German playwright who led the Berliner Ensemble theatre company.

clue.text: Literary traveller initially altered Eliot's character

indicators.note: initially altered means the opening letter of the word is replaced by another

parts.note: Lemuel Gulliver is Swift's travelling hero

explanation.surface: A fictional voyager is changed at the start into a George Eliot figure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'initially altered' swaps the G of GULLIVER for T.
explanation.definitionFit: Maggie and Tom Tulliver are the central siblings in George Eliot's The Mill on the Floss.

clue.text: Conceals in hand, holding second book of verses

indicators.note: holding means the word keeps the next piece within it

parts.note: a conjuror palms a card when hiding it in the hand

explanation.surface: Someone hides a second book of poetry in their hand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'holding' sets S inside PALMS.
explanation.definitionFit: The Book of Psalms is the biblical book of sacred songs, written in verse.

clue.text: French satirist represented as base liar

indicators.note: represented as means the letters are presented anew in a different order

explanation.surface: A French satirist is depicted as a low-down fibber.
explanation.walkthrough: 'represented as' rearranges BASELIAR.
explanation.definitionFit: François Rabelais wrote the satirical Gargantua and Pantagruel.

clue.text: Writer in state capital, speaking

indicators.note: speaking means the word is said out loud and matched to one that sounds alike

parts.note: Austin is the capital of Texas

explanation.surface: A writer lives in a seat of state government.
explanation.walkthrough: 'speaking' marks the soundalike: AUSTIN, the Texas capital, sounds like Jane Austen.
explanation.definitionFit: Jane Austen was the English novelist of Pride and Prejudice.

clue.text: It sounds like strong material, appropriate for magazine editor

indicators.note: it sounds like signals that a word said out loud matches the answer

parts.note: steel is a strong alloy

explanation.surface: Something tough-sounding is said to suit an editor of a periodical.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It sounds like' marks the homophone. Richard Steele founded and edited The Tatler and co-edited The Spectator.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Richard Steele edited the early eighteenth-century periodicals The Tatler and The Spectator.

clue.text: Recipient of literary journal, say, in South Africa

indicators.note: in means the next piece goes inside the two letters

parts.note: to tell is to say

explanation.surface: Someone in South Africa receives a literary periodical, so to speak.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' signals the container. Swift's Journal to Stella was a set of letters to Esther Johnson, not a magazine.
explanation.definitionFit: Jonathan Swift's Journal to Stella was addressed to Esther Johnson, whom he called by that name.

clue.text: Author's drunken scrawl I found in poem

indicators.note: found in means the rearranged letters sit inside the next piece

parts.note: an ode is a lyric poem

indicators.note: drunken means unsteady, so the letters stagger into a new order

explanation.surface: A writer's inebriated scribble turns up in a piece of verse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drunken' rearranges SCRAWLI into SCARWIL, and 'found in' places it inside ODE. The 's stands for 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Oscar Wilde was the Irish playwright and author of The Picture of Dorian Gray.

clue.text: Kingsley, the author, inappropriately abridged

indicators.note: abridged means shortened, so the last letter of the word is cut off

parts.note: amiss means wrongly or inappropriately

explanation.surface: Novelist Kingsley's work has been shortened unsuitably.
explanation.walkthrough: 'abridged' drops the final S of AMISS.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Kingsley Amis wrote Lucky Jim and other comic novels.

clue.text: Source of dark horse in best-seller list

definitions.text: Source of dark horse in best-seller list

parts.words: Source of dark horse in best-seller list
parts.note: the dark horse is a famous black horse of fiction, and its source is the woman who wrote that hugely popular novel

explanation.walkthrough: 'dark horse' usually means an unexpected contender; here it is literal, the horse Black Beauty, whose author's book sold in millions.
explanation.definitionFit: Anna Sewell wrote Black Beauty, one of the best-selling novels ever, about a black horse.

clue.text: See 24 down
Modern US writer is more sensible, holding nothing back

indicators.note: holding means the word keeps the next piece within it

parts.note: sager means wiser, more sensible

indicators.note: back means the word is read in reverse

parts.note: nil means nothing

explanation.surface: A recent American author is wiser, keeping nothing in reserve.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' signals the reversal and 'holding' the container; 'is' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: J. D. Salinger was a twentieth-century American novelist, author of The Catcher in the Rye.
